entries.test: Congressional legislative records and the proposed budget provision would establish existing federal AI protections and the scope and duration of the proposed preemption.
entries.note: The factual core is checkable; 'a major step backwards' is an accompanying value judgment.
'Likely' expressly hedges the constitutional claim.
'Deeply problematic' and 'especially dangerous' express an assessment of the policy.

entries.test: The proposed federal provision and the cited state election-deepfake and Colorado AI laws would establish whether enactment would block their enforcement without replacement protections.
entries.note: The antecedent is explicit in the surrounding paragraph; the claimed legal scope can be assessed from the texts.
The principal commitment is about how federal and state authority should be allocated.

entries.test: If the provision becomes law, public court dockets would show whether challenges to its constitutionality continue for years.
entries.note: Enactment is a reasonable contextual antecedent. The normalization narrows the predicted lawsuits to disputes over the interstate-commerce justification.

entries.test: If the described convergence continues, public comparisons of leading US and Chinese models would show whether either country establishes a sustained, substantial capability lead.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a plain reading of victory as durable technological superiority.

entries.test: Published model documentation, comparative evaluations, and research on shared architectures, training methods, and data would test whether those similarities explain convergence in US and Chinese model performance.
entries.note: Establishing causation is harder than establishing convergence, but public evidence can address both.

entries.test: Archived major AI leaderboards around May 14, 2025 would show the national distribution of the leading models.
Successive public model evaluations would show whether either country gains a substantial, persistent generative-AI capability advantage.
entries.note: A substantial and sustained national lead would contradict the prediction.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures and documented industry revenue and cost estimates through May 14, 2025 would show whether generative AI had produced an aggregate net profit.
entries.note: The net-profit assertion supplies a factual core despite the evaluative description 'speculative.'

entries.test: Public evaluations of successive leading US and Chinese AI products would show whether each side matches the other's capabilities or a durable capability gap emerges.
entries.note: The context makes 'match' a claim about competitive AI capabilities.

entries.test: Public compliance-cost disclosures and evidence linking regulatory changes to investment and model performance would show whether regulation remains a minor absorbed cost or materially affects US-China competitive outcomes.
entries.note: The normalization turns 'no serious argument' for an impact into an unqualified prediction of no impact. It also extends 'trivial for trillion dollar companies' to large firms generally.
'Probably' makes the outcome probabilistic. The normalization resolves the ambiguous 'it' specifically as lighter regulation.

entries.test: National AI regulations and historical model-performance comparisons through May 14, 2025 would show whether China regulated more extensively while narrowing its capability gap with the US.
entries.note: The claim says regulation did not prevent catching up; it does not require showing that regulation had no effect whatsoever.

entries.test: Federal statutes and executive orders in force on May 14, 2025 would establish whether enduring federal AI regulation was essentially absent.
entries.note: 'Washington has failed' accompanies a concrete assertion about federal legislation.
The passage explicitly calls passage of such legislation unlikely.
'Risk setting' asserts a possible consequence, rather than a firm outcome.

entries.test: State and territorial legislative records for 2024 would establish the counts adopting AI legislation or resolutions and passing deepfake laws.
entries.note: The normalization drops 'or resolutions,' making the 31-state assertion narrower and stronger.

entries.test: The proposed preemption text, existing state privacy statutes, and federal legislative records would establish whether every state privacy law would be displaced and whether a federal replacement had passed.
entries.note: The universal claim about state privacy laws is testable against the provision's scope and exceptions.
The claim identifies Big Tech's specific underlying motive, rather than merely its publicly observable lobbying activity.

entries.test: Public evidence from unregulated AI markets would show companies' safety and transparency incentives and whether resulting harms are paid for by companies or externalized to society.
entries.note: This is a prospective claim about an observable policy condition and its consequences.

entries.test: Public investigations and documented outcomes of industry self-regulation would show whether it repeatedly failed to deliver promised public protections.
entries.note: Repeated failures to provide promised protections give the assertion a testable plain reading.

entries.test: If AI oversight is absent or removed, lobbying disclosures and public policy submissions would show whether industry efforts to preserve weak accountability increase.

entries.note: This is a recommendation against federal preemption.
'Abdication of responsibility' is an asserted judgment of the policy's worth.

entries.test: Following enactment under the stated conditions, public legislation and enforcement records would show whether AI regulation is blocked for at least ten years.
entries.note: The decade-long closure is a firm, testable core. Being 'at Silicon Valley's mercy' is rhetorical emphasis.
This is an explicit call for political action.
